title: Socrates' last day
hook: Athens, 399 BCE: he spends his final hours talking with friends about the soul (Plato, Phaedo)
tomorrow: I know that I don't know

segments.voice: Yesterday, the raft: for crossing over, not for carrying on your head. Your line was leave the raft. What did you set down on the bank? Day eighty-five.

A new week, and a week of ordinary saints: people who weren't kings or prophets, just people who lived their questions all the way through. Here's a question people ask at parties: if you knew it was your last day, how would you spend it? Most answers involve a beach, or a big meal, or calling everyone you love. In Athens, in the year 399 BCE, a seventy-year-old man actually knew. And he spent it doing exactly what he'd done every other day of his life. He talked with his friends, and he asked questions. Today's story is Socrates' last day.
screen: `A WEEK OF ORDINARY SAINTS.` → `IF IT WERE YOUR LAST DAY.` → `ATHENS, 399 BCE.`

segments.voice: Socrates had been put on trial by his own city, charged with not honoring the city's gods and with corrupting the young. A jury of Athenians found him guilty and sentenced him to death. But a sacred ship had just sailed to the island of Delos, and by custom no one could be executed until it came back. So he waited about a month in prison, and his friends came every day. His student Plato wrote about the last of those days in a dialogue called the Phaedo. And in it Plato says, quietly, that he himself wasn't there; he was sick. So it's a story told by a friend, about what friends told him. That morning, the chains come off, and Socrates rubs his leg and remarks how pleasure and pain seem joined together, adding that Aesop could have made a fable out of it. He'd even been turning Aesop's fables into verse in his cell. Then, all day long, he talks with his friends about the soul, and whether it survives death. Two of them, Simmias and Cebes, raise hard objections. And Socrates doesn't get defensive. He welcomes them. Don't agree with me to be kind, he tells them, more or less; follow the argument. At sunset, he bathes, says goodbye to his family, and calmly drinks the poison the city has prepared. His last words are a small, strange request to his friend Crito: to pay a debt, a rooster owed to the god of healing. People still argue about what that meant. What stays is the picture. With hours left, he wasn't settling things. He was still asking, and still glad to be asked.
screen: `THE TRIAL AND THE SACRED SHIP.` · `PLATO WASN'T THERE; HE WAS ILL.` · `A LAST DAY OF HARD QUESTIONS.` · `THE CUP AT SUNSET.` · then, large: `KEEP ASKING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: have one real conversation today. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you'll probably talk to today. Not the easiest person, and not the hardest; someone in between. Now think of one real question you could ask them, not about logistics, but about what they think, or what they're wondering about lately. Picture asking it. Picture listening to the answer without rushing to agree or correct. Socrates' friends disagreed with him on his last day, and he was glad. The bell holds the time.
Socrates' last day. A whole final day spent in conversation about the soul, welcoming hard questions, until the sunset. Today's word.
Your line: keep asking. Today, ask one person one real question, and let their answer change your mind a little if it wants to. Day eighty-five.

howItsDone: Philosophy students often read the Phaedo as their first encounter with Socrates, and his calm, questioning last day is remembered across many traditions as a model of facing death with a clear mind.

myth: Plato was at Socrates' side at the end
in the Phaedo, Plato says he was ill and not there.
Socrates had been putting Aesop's fables into verse in prison
and he joked that Aesop could have made a fable of pleasure and pain.
Socrates asked his friends to agree with him
he welcomed their objections and told them to follow the argument.

fork.setup: you're Socrates, with one day left. your friends Simmias and Cebes start picking holes in your argument about the soul. what do you do?
options: ask them to let you have your last day in peace
welcome the objections and keep reasoning
change the subject to lighter things
fork.reveal: he welcomes them and keeps reasoning with them all day. he asks them to follow the argument, not to agree with him out of kindness.

original.note: Greek: psyche, soul, the breath of life. what Socrates and his friends talked about all day.

trapdoor: what you thought: a philosopher who calmly drank poison.
what it means: a man who spent his last day doing what he always did: asking, and welcoming questions.
what a scholar hears: Plato says in the Phaedo that he was ill and absent; the account is a friend's retelling.

notes: Phaedo paraphrased (Jowett's 1871 translation is public domain but not on the validator's list). Confirm: the Delos ship delay (58a–c), Plato's absence through illness (59b), the leg and Aesop remark and versifying Aesop (60b–61b), Simmias and Cebes's objections, the cock owed to Asclepius (118a).
The poison is traditionally hemlock; the Phaedo calls it the drug (pharmakon). The script says 'the poison'.
'About a month': Xenophon (Memorabilia 4.8.2) says thirty days; confirm.
